old: Triple-H therapy (hypertension, hypervolemia, hemodilution) for symptomatic vasospasm
new: Prophylactic triple-H therapy is no longer recommended; maintain euvolemia and consider induced hypertension only for delayed cerebral ischemia
rationale: Triple-H (hypervolemia/hemodilution) was abandoned; the 2023 AHA/ASA aSAH guideline recommends euvolemia and does not support prophylactic hypervolemia or hemodilution.
subject: Neurology

old: Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) or gabapentin for treatment
new: AASM 2024: gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin or pregabalin are preferred, plus IV ferric carboxymaltose if iron-deficient; standard use of dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) is now conditionally recommended against because of augmentation
rationale: The 2024 AASM RLS guideline reversed the 2012 position and no longer endorses dopamine agonists as first-line therapy.
subject: Neurology

old: Check serum ferritin — treat iron deficiency if ferritin <75. Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) or gabapentin first-line.
new: Check serum ferritin — treat iron deficiency if ferritin <75. AASM 2024: gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin, gabapentin enacarbil) are first-line and IV ferric carboxymaltose is preferred when iron-deficient; dopamine agonists are no longer recommended for standard use (augmentation risk).
subject: Psychiatry

old: Dopamine agonists or gabapentin/pregabalin are first-line
new: Gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin or pregabalin are first-line (AASM 2024); dopamine agonists are conditionally recommended against
subject: Psychiatry

old: tPA within 4.5 hours of symptom onset if no contraindications. BP must be <185/110 before administration.
new: IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset if no contraindications. BP must be <185/110 before administration.
rationale: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is now an accepted alternative (FDA labeled it for acute ischemic stroke in 2025); the alteplase-only wording is incomplete, not wrong.
subject: Neurology

old: Treatment: RIPE therapy + dexamethasone for severe cases
new: Treatment: RIPE therapy + adjunctive dexamethasone (recommended for TB meningitis generally, not only severe cases)
rationale: ATS/CDC/IDSA 2016 recommends adjunctive corticosteroids for TB meningitis; restricting them to severe disease is outdated.
subject: Neurology

old: Acute BP control: target SBP <140 within 1 hour
new: Acute BP control (AHA/ASA 2022): lower SBP toward 140 mmHg and keep it in the 130-150 range; avoid SBP <130
rationale: The 2022 ICH guideline specifies a 130-150 mmHg range and warns against intensive lowering below 130.
subject: Neurology

old: GBM: most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults. WHO grade IV. Pseudopalisading necrosis on histology.
new: GBM: most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults. IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 (WHO 2021). Pseudopalisading necrosis on histology.
rationale: WHO CNS5 restricts the term glioblastoma to IDH-wildtype tumors; IDH-mutant astrocytomas are no longer called GBM.
subject: Neurology

old: New LBBB + chest pain = STEMI equivalent
new: New LBBB alone is no longer a STEMI equivalent; apply (modified) Sgarbossa criteria and clinical judgment
rationale: The 2013 STEMI guideline and the 2021/2025 chest pain and ACS guidelines removed isolated new LBBB as an automatic STEMI equivalent. The deck also contradicts itself (c156 already says this).
subject: Cardiology

old: LBBB: broad notched R in lateral leads. New LBBB + chest pain = STEMI equivalent. Treat as STEMI.
new: LBBB: broad notched R in lateral leads. New LBBB with chest pain is not by itself a STEMI equivalent in current guidelines; use (modified) Sgarbossa criteria and clinical judgment.
subject: Cardiology

old: New LBBB + chest pain = treat as STEMI
new: New LBBB + chest pain: apply Sgarbossa criteria; not an automatic STEMI equivalent
subject: Cardiology

old: STEMI equivalents: new LBBB + chest pain, posterior MI, de Winter T waves
new: STEMI equivalents: posterior MI, de Winter T waves, Sgarbossa-positive LBBB or paced rhythm (new LBBB alone no longer qualifies)
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: Standard HF therapy but avoid ACEi/ARBs if breastfeeding
new: Standard HF therapy postpartum; ACEi/ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy, but enalapril and captopril are acceptable during breastfeeding
rationale: Enalapril/captopril are compatible with lactation; the blanket warning is not supported.
subject: Cardiology

old: RCRI: IHD, CHF, CVA/TIA, DM on insulin, CrCl ≤2, high-risk surgery. If ≥4 METs without symptoms → proceed to surgery without further testing.
new: RCRI: IHD, CHF, CVA/TIA, DM on insulin, serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL, high-risk surgery. If ≥4 METs without symptoms → proceed to surgery without further testing.
rationale: The RCRI renal criterion is preoperative serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL; "CrCl ≤2" is not a valid threshold.
subject: Cardiology

old: Stable demand ischemia. Stress test for diagnosis. Medical therapy: aspirin, statin, beta-blocker, nitrate.
new: Stable demand ischemia. Initial testing: coronary CTA or stress imaging (CCTA is favored for many patients without known CAD). Medical therapy: aspirin, statin, plus a beta-blocker or CCB (± long-acting nitrate) for symptom control.
rationale: 2021 AHA/ACC chest pain and 2023 chronic coronary disease guidelines favor CCTA or stress imaging; beta-blockers improve outcomes mainly after MI or with reduced EF.
subject: Cardiology

old: Stress test is initial diagnostic test in stable angina
new: Coronary CTA or stress testing (ECG or imaging) is the initial evaluation of stable chest pain (2021 AHA/ACC)
subject: Cardiology

old: Medical therapy: aspirin + statin + beta-blocker ± long-acting nitrate
new: Antianginals: beta-blocker or CCB first; add long-acting nitrate or ranolazine; beta-blockers improve outcomes mainly after MI or with EF ≤50%
subject: Cardiology

old: Exercise stress test is first-line for stable angina evaluation
new: Exercise ECG stress testing is one option for stable chest pain; coronary CTA or stress imaging are preferred in many patients (2021 AHA/ACC)
subject: Cardiology

old: Duke criteria: 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor. Blood cultures + echo. Empiric vanc + gent.
new: Duke criteria: 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor. Blood cultures + echo. Empiric therapy per AHA/ESC: vancomycin plus a second agent chosen by risk (for example ceftriaxone or cefepime); routine gentamicin is no longer favored for staphylococcal native-valve IE. Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria are the current update.
rationale: AHA 2015 and ESC 2023 de-emphasize gentamicin for staphylococcal native-valve endocarditis; regimen choice depends on risk and local resistance.
subject: Cardiology

old: JNC 8/ACC 2017: thiazide, CCB, ACEi, or ARB for uncomplicated HTN. Target <130/80 for most adults.
new: 2025 AHA/ACC: thiazide-type diuretic, ACEi/ARB, or dihydropyridine CCB first-line; a two-drug single-pill combination is preferred for stage 2 (≥140/90). Target <130/80 for most adults.
rationale: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline replaced the 2017 document (JNC 8 was never an ACC/AHA guideline).
subject: Cardiology

old: African Americans: thiazide or CCB preferred (not ACEi/ARB monotherapy)
new: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline no longer recommends different first-line drugs by race; choose by comorbidities (ACEi/ARB for albuminuric CKD or diabetes)
rationale: Race-based first-line selection was dropped in 2025.
subject: Cardiology

old: 2017 ACC/AHA: Stage 1 HTN = 130-139/80-89. Stage 2 = ≥140/90. Confirm with out-of-office measurements. Lifestyle for Stage 1 low-risk; meds if high-risk or Stage 2.
new: 2017 ACC/AHA: Stage 1 HTN = 130-139/80-89. Stage 2 = ≥140/90. Confirm with out-of-office measurements. Stage 1: start drugs if PREVENT 10-year CVD risk ≥7.5% or established CVD/diabetes/CKD (2025 AHA/ACC keeps the 2017 categories); Stage 2: two-drug combination.
rationale: Title/body cite the 2017 guideline; the 2025 guideline keeps categories but changes treatment initiation (PREVENT).
subject: Cardiology

old: Four statin benefit groups: clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥190, diabetes 40-75, 10-year ASCVD risk ≥7.5%. High-intensity: atorvastatin 40-80mg or rosuvastatin 20-40mg.
new: Four statin benefit groups (2018 ACC/AHA): clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥190, diabetes 40-75, 10-year risk ≥7.5%. The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline now uses PREVENT risk (statin indicated from about 5% 10-year risk) and restores LDL-C goals (<70 mg/dL in ASCVD, <55 in very high risk). Verify against the guideline text before adopting. High-intensity: atorvastatin 40-80mg or rosuvastatin 20-40mg.
rationale: A 2026 guideline superseded the 2018 thresholds the card teaches. Exam boards may still test 2018; consider dual-labeling.
subject: Cardiology

old: Target BP <140/90 (or <135/85 per CHAP trial)
new: CHAP trial: treating chronic hypertension at ≥140/90 (goal <140/90) improved pregnancy outcomes; verify the <135/85 figure before keeping it
rationale: The <135/85 number could not be verified against CHAP; keep only after checking.
subject: Cardiology

old: Group 1 (PAH): PCWP ≤15 and PVR ≥3 Wood units
new: Group 1 (PAH): PCWP ≤15 and PVR >2 Wood units (2022 ESC/ERS; older criterion ≥3)
rationale: 2022 ESC/ERS lowered the precapillary PH PVR threshold to >2 WU.
subject: Cardiology

old: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa reverses Xa inhibitors
new: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; 4-factor PCC is used for life-threatening Xa-inhibitor bleeding (andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025)
rationale: AstraZeneca withdrew Andexxa from the US after thrombosis concerns (ANNEXA-I).
subject: Cardiology

old: Andexanet alfa reverses Xa inhibitors
new: 4-factor PCC is used for life-threatening Xa-inhibitor bleeding (andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025)
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: Emergent reversal: warfarin → IV vitamin K + 4-factor PCC (or FFP). DOAC → idarucizumab (dabigatran) or andexanet alfa (Xa inhibitors).
new: Emergent reversal: warfarin → IV vitamin K + 4-factor PCC (or FFP). DOAC → idarucizumab (dabigatran) or 4-factor PCC for Xa inhibitors (andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025).
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban)
new: Andexanet alfa (no longer marketed in the US since December 2025) reverses factor Xa inhibitors; 4F-PCC is the US alternative
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: Treat urgently: IV calcium gluconate (stabilize membrane) → insulin + glucose (shift K into cells) → kayexalate/patiromer (remove K). Dialysis if refractory.
new: Treat urgently: IV calcium gluconate (stabilize membrane) → insulin + glucose (shift K into cells) → a K binder such as sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer (sodium polystyrene sulfonate is slow and falling out of favor) (remove K). Dialysis if refractory.
rationale: SPS carries bowel-necrosis warnings and slow onset; newer binders are preferred. Low-priority modernization.
subject: Cardiology

old: Digibind (Fab fragments) is antidote — also binds and lowers K
new: Digoxin-specific Fab (DigiFab; the Digibind brand is discontinued) is the antidote; reversing Na/K-ATPase inhibition also lowers K
subject: Cardiology

old: HRS: functional renal failure in advanced liver disease. FeNa <1%. Liver transplant definitive. Midodrine + octreotide bridge.
new: HRS: functional renal failure in advanced liver disease. FeNa <1%. Liver transplant definitive. Albumin plus a vasoconstrictor: terlipressin (FDA-approved 2022) or norepinephrine preferred; midodrine + octreotide is a less effective alternative.
rationale: AASLD 2021 guidance prefers terlipressin/norepinephrine with albumin for HRS-AKI.
subject: Nephrology

old: HRS: functional renal failure in advanced liver disease. FeNa <1% (kidneys structurally normal). Liver transplant definitive. Bridge: midodrine + octreotide + albumin.
new: HRS: functional renal failure in advanced liver disease. FeNa <1% (kidneys structurally normal). Liver transplant definitive. Treatment: albumin + terlipressin (or norepinephrine); midodrine + octreotide + albumin is a less effective alternative.
subject: Nephrology

old: Rapidly progressive renal failure in advanced cirrhosis. Diagnosis of exclusion. Type 1: creatinine doubles in <2 weeks. Bridge: midodrine + octreotide + albumin. Liver transplant definitive.
new: Rapidly progressive renal failure in advanced cirrhosis. Diagnosis of exclusion. Type 1: creatinine doubles in <2 weeks. Treatment: albumin + terlipressin (or norepinephrine); midodrine + octreotide + albumin is a less effective alternative. Liver transplant definitive.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: ACEi/ARBs are Category X in pregnancy — absolute contraindication
new: ACEi/ARBs carry a boxed warning for fetal toxicity (FDA letter categories were retired in 2015) — contraindicated in pregnancy
subject: Nephrology

old: Keep Ca x P product <55 to prevent metastatic calcification
new: Older teaching: keep Ca × P <55; KDIGO CKD-MBD no longer uses the product and targets individual calcium, phosphate and PTH values
subject: Nephrology

old: Target Hgb 10-11 g/dL — avoid >13 (thrombosis risk)
new: Use the lowest ESA dose that avoids transfusion; KDIGO advises not to intentionally exceed Hgb 11.5 g/dL (higher targets raise stroke and CV risk)
rationale: The ">13" cut is far above current labeling/KDIGO caution.
subject: Nephrology

old: <5mm stones pass spontaneously ~90% of the time
new: Stones <5 mm pass spontaneously in roughly two-thirds or more of patients (pooled estimate ~68%; ~47% for 5-10 mm)
rationale: The 90% figure overstates published passage rates.
subject: Nephrology

old: Stones <5mm usually pass spontaneously (90%). Hydration + NSAIDs for pain. Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) for medical expulsive therapy.
new: Stones <5mm usually pass spontaneously (about two-thirds or more). Hydration + NSAIDs for pain. Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) for medical expulsive therapy.
subject: Nephrology

old: Tamsulosin relaxes ureteral smooth muscle to aid passage
new: Tamsulosin relaxes ureteral smooth muscle, but trials (SUSPEND, STONE) showed little benefit; any benefit is mainly for larger (>5 mm) distal stones
rationale: Evidence for medical expulsive therapy is mixed.
subject: Nephrology

old: <5mm stones: 90% pass spontaneously. >10mm: almost always need intervention
new: <5mm stones: roughly two-thirds or more pass spontaneously (about half for 5-10 mm). >10mm: almost always need intervention
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: WBC casts localize infection to kidney. Treat fluoroquinolones or TMP-SMX. Urine culture confirms.
new: WBC casts localize infection to kidney. Outpatient: fluoroquinolone only if local resistance is <10%, otherwise a ceftriaxone dose then culture-directed oral therapy (TMP-SMX or a beta-lactam). Urine culture confirms.
rationale: Rising fluoroquinolone/TMP-SMX resistance changes empiric choices.
subject: Nephrology

old: E. coli most common cause. WBC casts localize to kidney. Treat: fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX for 7-14 days outpatient; IV ceftriaxone if inpatient.
new: E. coli most common cause. WBC casts localize to kidney. Outpatient: culture-directed therapy (fluoroquinolone 7 days or TMP-SMX 14 days if susceptible; otherwise a ceftriaxone dose then an oral beta-lactam); IV ceftriaxone if inpatient.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: CKD-EPI is preferred over MDRD for GFR estimation
new: CKD-EPI (2021 race-free creatinine and creatinine-cystatin C equations) is preferred over MDRD; race is no longer used
subject: Nephrology

old: Most common cause of secondary hypertension
new: Most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension (2025 Endocrine Society guideline suggests screening all adults with hypertension)
rationale: Primary aldosteronism is the leading endocrine cause; OSA and renal disease are also very common.
subject: Nephrology

old: Most common cause of secondary hypertension
new: Most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension (2025 Endocrine Society guideline suggests screening all adults with hypertension)
subject: Endocrinology

old: Spironolactone must be stopped 6 weeks before testing
new: Older protocol: stop spironolactone about 4-6 weeks before testing; the 2025 Endocrine Society guideline suggests screening can often proceed on most antihypertensives (verify against the guideline)
rationale: Testing-condition advice was relaxed in 2025; confirm exact wording before adopting.
subject: Endocrinology

old: REMS program: mandatory ANC monitoring (weekly → biweekly → monthly)
new: ANC monitoring is still required by the label (weekly for 6 months, then biweekly, then monthly); the Clozapine REMS program itself was eliminated by the FDA in 2025
rationale: FDA announced removal of the REMS in 2025; labeled ANC monitoring continues.
subject: Psychiatry

old: Excited Delirium
new: Severe Hyperactive Delirium (formerly "Excited Delirium")
rationale: ACEP withdrew its 2009 white paper (Oct 2023); "excited delirium" is not a recognized diagnosis.
subject: Psychiatry

old: Controversial entity. Agitation + hyperthermia + altered consciousness + often stimulant use. Risk of sudden cardiac death. Rapid sedation and cooling. Avoid prolonged physical restraint.
new: "Excited delirium" is not a recognized diagnosis (ACEP withdrew its 2009 white paper in 2023; AMA and APA reject the term). Modern framing: hyperactive delirium or severe agitation with hyperadrenergic features and hyperthermia. Treat as a medical emergency: rapid sedation, cooling, avoid prolonged prone restraint.
subject: Psychiatry

old: Most common personality disorder in clinical settings
new: OCPD is among the most prevalent personality disorders in the general population (borderline PD is the most common in clinical settings)
rationale: Borderline PD, not OCPD, predominates in clinical samples.
subject: Psychiatry

old: Cluster C: most commonly seen in clinical practice
new: Borderline (Cluster B) is the most common personality disorder in clinical settings; OCPD (Cluster C) is the most prevalent in community samples
subject: Psychiatry

old: Malingering is NOT a psychiatric diagnosis (it's a V-code)
new: Malingering is NOT a psychiatric diagnosis (it is coded as a Z-code: "other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention", ICD-10-CM Z76.5)
rationale: V-codes were replaced by ICD-10-CM Z-codes.
subject: Psychiatry

old: First-line: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin × 14 days. Bismuth quadruple therapy if penicillin allergic. Confirm eradication with urea breath test or stool antigen.
new: First-line (ACG 2024): optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole). Clarithromycin triple therapy only when clarithromycin susceptibility is documented. Alternatives: rifabutin triple or vonoprazan-based regimens. Confirm eradication with urea breath test or stool antigen.
rationale: ACG 2024 dropped empiric clarithromycin triple therapy as first-line because of US resistance.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Bismuth quadruple therapy is alternative if penicillin allergy
new: Bismuth quadruple therapy is the preferred first-line regimen in the US; it is essential in penicillin allergy
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
new: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD, formerly NAFLD)
rationale: The 2023 multisociety nomenclature renamed NAFLD to MASLD and NASH to MASH.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: NAFLD: most common liver disease worldwide. Can progress: steatosis → NASH → cirrhosis → HCC. Weight loss and exercise first-line.
new: MASLD (formerly NAFLD): most common liver disease worldwide. Can progress: steatosis → MASH (formerly NASH) → cirrhosis → HCC. Weight loss and exercise first-line; resmetirom is approved for noncirrhotic MASH with F2-F3 fibrosis.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: NASH (Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis)
new: MASH (Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis, formerly NASH)
subject: Gastroenterology

old: NASH = steatosis + inflammation + hepatocyte ballooning ± fibrosis. Diagnosis requires liver biopsy. Can progress to cirrhosis and HCC. Weight loss is cornerstone.
new: MASH (formerly NASH) = steatosis + inflammation + hepatocyte ballooning ± fibrosis. Diagnosis requires liver biopsy. Can progress to cirrhosis and HCC. Weight loss is cornerstone.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Low-risk adenoma (1-2, <10mm, tubular): repeat in 7-10 years. High-risk (≥3, ≥10mm, villous, HGD): repeat in 3 years. Serrated polyps: varies by size/location.
new: 2020 USMSTF: 1-2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7-10 years; 3-4 adenomas <10 mm: 3-5 years; 5-10 adenomas, or any adenoma ≥10 mm, villous histology or HGD: 3 years; >10 adenomas: 1 year. Serrated polyps: varies by size/location.
rationale: The 2020 update split the old 3-year "advanced" group; 3-4 small adenomas now get 3-5 years.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Low-risk: 7-10 years; high-risk: 3 years
new: 1-2 small tubular adenomas: 7-10 years; 3-4 small adenomas: 3-5 years; advanced adenoma or 5-10 adenomas: 3 years
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Carvedilol may be superior to propranolol (additional alpha-1 block)
new: Carvedilol is now preferred in compensated cirrhosis with clinically significant portal hypertension (Baveno VII; AASLD 2024)
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol, nadolol) for prophylaxis
new: Non-selective beta-blockers for prophylaxis; carvedilol is now preferred (propranolol or nadolol are alternatives)
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Encapsulated fluid collection without solid component, develops >4 weeks after interstitial edematous pancreatitis. Drain if symptomatic or >6cm.
new: Encapsulated fluid collection without solid component, develops >4 weeks after interstitial edematous pancreatitis. Drain only if symptomatic, infected or obstructing; size alone (>6 cm) is no longer an indication.
rationale: Modern pancreatic fluid collection management is symptom- and complication-driven.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Drain if symptomatic, infected, or >6cm
new: Drain if symptomatic, infected, or obstructing; size alone is not an indication
subject: Gastroenterology

old: GI relevance: allopurinol can cause hepatotoxicity; febuxostat preferred in CKD. Colchicine causes diarrhea (common GI side effect). NSAIDs risk GI bleed.
new: GI relevance: allopurinol can cause hepatotoxicity; allopurinol is first-line urate-lowering therapy even in CKD (ACR 2020); febuxostat is second-line. Colchicine causes diarrhea (common GI side effect). NSAIDs risk GI bleed.
rationale: ACR 2020 strongly prefers allopurinol over other xanthine oxidase inhibitors, including in CKD.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Febuxostat doesn't need renal dose adjustment
new: Febuxostat needs no dose adjustment in mild-moderate CKD but carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death
subject: Gastroenterology

old: TMP-SMX long-term treatment
new: Initial ceftriaxone (or meropenem) for about 2 weeks, then TMP-SMX for about 12 months
rationale: Current regimens use a parenteral induction phase before long-term TMP-SMX.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: MELD uses bilirubin, INR, and creatinine. Higher score = higher transplant priority. MELD-Na incorporates sodium for better prediction.
new: MELD uses bilirubin, INR, and creatinine. Higher score = higher transplant priority. MELD-Na incorporates sodium; MELD 3.0 (adopted by OPTN in July 2023) also adds albumin and female sex.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Inflammation of diverticulum. Left-sided appendicitis. CT with contrast diagnostic. Antibiotics ± drainage.
new: Inflammation of diverticulum. Left-sided appendicitis. CT with contrast diagnostic. Uncomplicated disease in immunocompetent patients can often be managed without antibiotics (AGA 2021); abscesses >3-4 cm need drainage plus antibiotics.
rationale: AGA 2021 recommends selective rather than routine antibiotics.
subject: Gastroenterology

old: Colonoscopy 6-8 weeks after resolution to rule out cancer
new: Colonoscopy after complicated diverticulitis (or if none is recent); routine colonoscopy after a first uncomplicated episode is no longer required
subject: Surgery

old: Step therapy: SABA PRN → low-dose ICS → ICS-LABA → high-dose ICS-LABA → biologics
new: GINA 2024 (age ≥12): preferred track is as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol at every step (± daily ICS-formoterol); SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended; biologics for severe asthma
rationale: The SABA-first stepwise ladder was retired by GINA (2019+) and NAEPP 2020.
subject: Pulmonology

old: Intermittent: SABA PRN only; persistent: add ICS
new: Ages 6-11: intermittent = SABA PRN (or ICS with each SABA use); persistent = daily low-dose ICS. Age ≥12: as-needed ICS-formoterol (GINA/NAEPP 2020)
subject: Pediatrics

old: Latent: positive test, negative CXR, asymptomatic. Treat with isoniazid 9 months (add pyridoxine/B6) or rifampin 4 months.
new: Latent: positive test, negative CXR, asymptomatic. CDC/NTCA 2020 preferred regimens: 3 months of weekly isoniazid + rifapentine (3HP), 4 months of rifampin (4R) or 3 months of daily isoniazid + rifampin (3HR); 6-9 months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) is an alternative.
rationale: Short rifamycin-based regimens are now preferred over 9 months of isoniazid.
subject: Pulmonology

old: Latent TB: positive PPD/IGRA, negative CXR, asymptomatic. Treat to prevent reactivation. INH × 9 months (+ B6) OR rifampin × 4 months. Do NOT treat with RIPE.
new: Latent TB: positive PPD/IGRA, negative CXR, asymptomatic. Treat to prevent reactivation. Preferred: 3HP, 4R or 3HR (CDC/NTCA 2020); alternatives: INH 6-9 months (+ B6). Do NOT treat with RIPE.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: INH × 9 months is standard; always add pyridoxine (B6)
new: Short-course rifamycin regimens (3HP, 4R, 3HR) are preferred; if INH is used (6-9 months), add pyridoxine (B6)
subject: Infectious Disease

old: RSV most common cause. <2 years old. Supportive care (suctioning, O2). Palivizumab prophylaxis for high-risk infants.
new: RSV most common cause. <2 years old. Supportive care (suctioning, O2). Prevention: nirsevimab (or clesrovimab) for infants <8 months entering their first RSV season, or maternal RSV vaccine at 32-36 weeks; palivizumab only for select high-risk infants when those are unavailable.
rationale: Long-acting RSV monoclonals and the maternal vaccine now cover most infants.
subject: Pulmonology

old: Palivizumab prophylaxis for premature infants and those with CHD/BPD
new: Nirsevimab/clesrovimab (single dose) or maternal RSV vaccine now cover most infants; palivizumab (monthly) is reserved for select high-risk infants
subject: Pulmonology

old: RSV most common cause. Supportive care (suctioning, O2). Palivizumab prophylaxis for high-risk infants (premature, CHD, BPD).
new: RSV most common cause. Supportive care (suctioning, O2). Prevention: nirsevimab or clesrovimab for infants <8 months in their first RSV season (or maternal RSV vaccine); palivizumab only for select high-risk infants.
subject: Pediatrics

old: Palivizumab for high-risk infants (premature <29wk, CHD, BPD)
new: Nirsevimab/clesrovimab now cover most infants; palivizumab only for select high-risk infants
subject: Pediatrics

old: LAMA (tiotropium, umeclidinium) first-line maintenance for COPD. Reduces exacerbations. Different from short-acting ipratropium.
new: GOLD 2024: LABA + LAMA is initial therapy for Group B and E (LAMA alone is acceptable for Group A); add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 in Group E. LAMA examples: tiotropium, umeclidinium. Reduces exacerbations. Different from short-acting ipratropium.
subject: Pulmonology

old: GOLD guidelines: LAMA or LABA first-line maintenance
new: GOLD 2024: Group B/E start LABA + LAMA; consider ICS with eosinophils ≥300
subject: Pulmonology

old: Most common type (85%): proximal esophageal atresia with distal TEF (H-type). NG tube coils in proximal pouch. Polyhydramnios in utero.
new: Most common type (85%): proximal esophageal atresia with distal TEF (Gross type C). NG tube coils in proximal pouch. Polyhydramnios in utero.
source: Internal contradiction with pe097/pe182 in this deck; Gross classification of esophageal atresia (no URL)
rationale: H-type fistula is a different, rare entity without atresia (pe182); the card contradicts itself.
subject: Pulmonology

old: CDC recommends PCV15 followed by PPSV23 (or PCV20 alone) for adults ≥65 or immunocompromised or with chronic conditions. Prevents invasive pneumococcal disease.
new: CDC/ACIP (Oct 2024; MMWR Jan 2025): one dose of PCV20 or PCV21 (or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) for all adults ≥50 without prior PCV, and for ages 19-49 with risk conditions or immunocompromise. Prevents invasive pneumococcal disease.
rationale: ACIP lowered the universal age to 50 and added PCV21.
subject: Pulmonology

old: PCV15 → PPSV23 sequence for broader serotype coverage
new: PCV15 must be followed by PPSV23; PCV20 or PCV21 alone completes the series
subject: Pulmonology

old: All adults ≥65 and high-risk younger adults should receive
new: All adults ≥50 and high-risk adults 19-49 should receive
subject: Pulmonology

old: PCV15 or PCV20 for all adults ≥65 (updated 2023). If PCV15 given, follow with PPSV23. Also for immunocompromised, asplenic, CSF leak, cochlear implant at any age.
new: PCV20 or PCV21 (or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) for all adults ≥50 (ACIP Oct 2024; MMWR Jan 2025). Also for immunocompromised, asplenic, CSF leak, cochlear implant at any age.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: All adults ≥65 and high-risk younger adults
new: All adults ≥50 and high-risk adults 19-49
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Vaccinate at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy: pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), meningococcal (MenACWY + MenB), Hib. Daily penicillin prophylaxis in children.
new: Vaccinate at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy: pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV21 alone, or PCV15 + PPSV23; PCV13 is no longer used), meningococcal (MenACWY + MenB), Hib. Daily penicillin prophylaxis in children.
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: GBS: leading cause of neonatal sepsis/meningitis. Screen mothers at 35-37 weeks. Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis.
new: GBS: leading cause of neonatal sepsis/meningitis. Screen mothers at 36 0/7-37 6/7 weeks. Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis.
rationale: ACOG/CDC changed the window to 36 0/7-37 6/7 weeks in 2019-2020; pearl[0] and ob060 already say 36-37.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Often co-infects with Chlamydia. Treat both: ceftriaxone IM + doxycycline (or azithromycin). NAAT gold standard.
new: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Often co-infects with Chlamydia. Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once (1 g if ≥150 kg); add doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days if chlamydia is not excluded (CDC 2021). NAAT gold standard.
rationale: CDC 2021 recommends doxycycline, not azithromycin, for co-treatment of chlamydia.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Always treat for Chlamydia simultaneously
new: Treat for chlamydia too unless chlamydial infection has been excluded
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM single dose (updated 2020 CDC guidelines)
new: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose (CDC 2021 STI treatment guidelines)
subject: Infectious Disease

old: MAC: most common opportunistic mycobacterial infection in AIDS. Prophylaxis with azithromycin when CD4 <50. Treat with clarithromycin + ethambutol.
new: MAC: most common opportunistic mycobacterial infection in AIDS. Primary prophylaxis (azithromycin, CD4 <50) is not recommended if ART is started immediately. Treat with clarithromycin + ethambutol.
rationale: NIH OI guidelines no longer recommend primary MAC prophylaxis for patients starting ART immediately.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Prophylaxis with azithromycin when CD4 <50
new: Primary prophylaxis (azithromycin) only if ART cannot be started immediately and CD4 <50
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Vancomycin: binds D-Ala-D-Ala → inhibits cell wall synthesis. Red man syndrome is histamine release (not allergy) — slow infusion rate. Monitor trough levels.
new: Vancomycin: binds D-Ala-D-Ala → inhibits cell wall synthesis. Red man syndrome is histamine release (not allergy) — slow infusion rate. Monitor AUC (preferred) or trough levels.
rationale: 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP guideline replaced trough-only monitoring with AUC/MIC (400-600) dosing for serious MRSA infections.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Monitor trough levels (target 15-20 for serious infections)
new: AUC/MIC-guided dosing (AUC 400-600 mg·h/L) is preferred over trough-only monitoring (15-20) for serious MRSA infections (2020 consensus)
subject: Infectious Disease

old: First recurrence: fidaxomicin preferred or vancomycin taper/pulse. Second recurrence: fecal microbiota transplant (FMT). Bezlotoxumab for prevention of recurrence.
new: First recurrence: fidaxomicin preferred or vancomycin taper/pulse. Second recurrence: fecal microbiota transplant (FMT). Bezlotoxumab was discontinued by Merck in January 2025 and is no longer available.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B monoclonal antibody) prevents recurrence
new: Bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B antibody) reduced recurrence but was discontinued by the manufacturer in January 2025
subject: Infectious Disease

old: S. aureus is #1 in ALL populations (even sickle cell)
new: S. aureus is #1 overall; in sickle cell disease Salmonella is the classic board-tested pathogen (S. aureus remains common)
source: Internal contradiction with he088, rh161, pe197 in this deck; conventional board teaching: Salmonella in sickle cell osteomyelitis (no URL)
rationale: Contradicts he088/rh161/pe197; evidence in SCD is mixed but the board answer is Salmonella.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Osteomyelitis in SCD: Salmonella is #2 (S. aureus still #1)
new: Osteomyelitis in SCD: Salmonella is the classic board-tested pathogen (S. aureus remains common)
source: Internal contradiction with he088, rh161, pe197 in this deck; conventional board teaching: Salmonella in sickle cell osteomyelitis (no URL)
subject: Infectious Disease

old: qSOFA: altered mental status, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100. Hour-1 bundle: cultures, lactate, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors if refractory.
new: qSOFA: altered mental status, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100. Hour-1 bundle: cultures, lactate, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypoperfusion (weak recommendation in SSC 2021), vasopressors if refractory. SSC 2021 recommends against qSOFA as a single screening tool.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Most common HAI in the US
new: Among the most common HAIs (CDC prevalence surveys list pneumonia and surgical-site infection first)
rationale: Rank has changed in prevalence surveys.
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Rheumatic fever: ONLY from pharyngitis (never skin)
new: Rheumatic fever classically follows GAS pharyngitis; skin infection as a trigger is debated (Australian data)
source: Debated in the literature: Australian ARF guideline 2020 (RHDAustralia) vs AHA 2015 Jones criteria statement (no URL)
subject: Infectious Disease

old: Type 2 DM. Osmolarity >320. Higher mortality than DKA. IV fluids first priority, then insulin.
new: Type 2 DM. Effective osmolality ≥300 mOsm/kg (2024 ADA/EASD consensus; older teaching >320). Higher mortality than DKA. IV fluids first priority, then insulin.
subject: Endocrinology

old: Serum osmolarity >320 mOsm/kg is diagnostic
new: Effective serum osmolality ≥300 mOsm/kg (older teaching >320) with glucose ≥600 mg/dL and minimal ketosis
subject: Endocrinology

old: Metformin is first-line unless contraindicated
new: Metformin remains a common first agent, but ADA 2025 recommends a GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i with proven benefit for ASCVD, HF or CKD independent of A1c and metformin use
subject: Endocrinology

old: Metformin first-line. If CVD: add GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i. If CKD: SGLT2i. If HF: SGLT2i. If HbA1c still above target: add another agent.
new: ADA 2025: for ASCVD, HF or CKD start a GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2i with proven benefit regardless of A1c or metformin use; otherwise metformin is a common first agent; favor GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide when weight loss is a priority.
subject: Endocrinology

old: Diabetes is a coronary artery disease equivalent
new: Older teaching; current guidelines treat diabetes as a risk enhancer and stratify by age and risk factors rather than as a CAD equivalent
subject: Endocrinology

old: Recombinant PTH(1-34). Intermittent dosing stimulates osteoblast activity (anabolic). Continuous PTH = catabolic. Limited to 2 years (osteosarcoma risk in rats).
new: Recombinant PTH(1-34). Intermittent dosing stimulates osteoblast activity (anabolic). Continuous PTH = catabolic. Typically limited to about 2 years (the FDA removed the osteosarcoma boxed warning in 2020).
subject: Endocrinology

old: Increase levothyroxine by ~30% upon pregnancy confirmation. Monitor TSH every 4 weeks in first half, then at least once per trimester. Goal TSH <4 mIU/L.
new: Increase levothyroxine by ~30% upon pregnancy confirmation. Monitor TSH every 4 weeks in first half, then at least once per trimester. Goal TSH in the lower half of the trimester-specific reference range (or <2.5 mIU/L if unavailable) (ATA 2017).
rationale: ATA 2017 targets <2.5 when no local range exists.
subject: Endocrinology

old: Metformin and insulin are only FDA-approved for pediatric T2DM
new: Metformin, insulin, GLP-1 RAs (liraglutide, exenatide ER, dulaglutide) and SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) are now FDA-approved for pediatric T2DM (age ≥10)
subject: Endocrinology

old: Indications: BMI ≥40 or ≥35 with comorbidities (T2DM, OSA, HTN). Roux-en-Y: most weight loss but more complications. Sleeve: simpler, fewer deficiencies.
new: ASMBS/IFSO 2022: BMI ≥35 regardless of comorbidity; consider at BMI 30-34.9 with metabolic disease. Roux-en-Y: most weight loss but more complications. Sleeve: simpler, fewer deficiencies.
rationale: The 2022 guideline removed the comorbidity requirement.
subject: Endocrinology

old: Indications: BMI ≥40, or BMI ≥35 with obesity-related comorbidity (DM2, HTN, OSA). Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy most common.
new: ASMBS/IFSO 2022: BMI ≥35 regardless of comorbidity; consider at BMI 30-34.9 with metabolic disease. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy most common.
subject: Surgery

old: BMI ≥40 or ≥35 with comorbidity = eligible for bariatric surgery
new: BMI ≥35 (any comorbidity status) = eligible; consider 30-34.9 with metabolic disease (ASMBS/IFSO 2022)
subject: Surgery

old: Always rule out pheochromocytoma first (metanephrines)
new: Biochemical pheochromocytoma testing is needed unless unenhanced CT attenuation is ≤10 HU (ESE/ENSAT 2023); all need a 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test for autonomous cortisol
subject: Endocrinology

old: Rule out pheo in ALL cases (even if normotensive)
new: Screen for pheochromocytoma (metanephrines) if unenhanced CT is >10 HU; lipid-rich adenomas ≤10 HU can skip it (ESE/ENSAT 2023)
subject: Surgery

old: Hydroxyurea: increases HbF, reduces crises. Voxelotor: polymerization inhibitor, increases Hb. Crizanlizumab: anti-P-selectin, reduces vaso-occlusive events. L-glutamine: reduces oxidative stress.
new: Hydroxyurea: increases HbF, reduces crises. Voxelotor was withdrawn worldwide in September 2024 for safety (excess vaso-occlusive crises and deaths). Crizanlizumab (anti-P-selectin): phase 3 STAND did not show fewer crises and EU authorization was revoked. L-glutamine: reduces oxidative stress.
rationale: Two listed drugs are withdrawn or unproven.
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: Crizanlizumab (anti-P-selectin) is newer addition for VOC prevention
new: Crizanlizumab's benefit was not confirmed in phase 3 (STAND)
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: MDS/MPN overlap syndrome. Persistent peripheral monocytosis >1 × 10⁹/L for >3 months. Dysplastic features. Can transform to AML. Treat with hypomethylating agents or allogeneic BMT.
new: MDS/MPN overlap syndrome. Persistent absolute monocytosis ≥0.5 × 10⁹/L with monocytes ≥10% of WBC (WHO 5th ed./ICC 2022; WHO 2016 used ≥1 × 10⁹/L). Dysplastic features. Can transform to AML. Treat with hypomethylating agents or allogeneic BMT.
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: Ferrous sulfate 325mg (65mg elemental iron) TID on empty stomach. Vitamin C enhances absorption. GI side effects (nausea, constipation) are most common reason for non-compliance. Reticulocyte count should rise within 1 week.
new: Ferrous sulfate 325mg (65mg elemental iron) once daily or on alternate days (better fractional absorption and tolerance than TID). Vitamin C enhances absorption. GI side effects (nausea, constipation) are most common reason for non-compliance. Reticulocyte count should rise within 1 week.
rationale: Hepcidin physiology favors single daily or alternate-day dosing.
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: Protamine is a positively charged protein that binds negatively charged heparin. 1mg protamine per 100 units heparin. Partially reverses LMWH (anti-IIa but not anti-Xa activity).
new: Protamine is a positively charged protein that binds negatively charged heparin. 1mg protamine per 100 units heparin. Fully reverses unfractionated heparin; only partially reverses LMWH (neutralizes anti-IIa but only about 60% of anti-Xa activity).
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: Monoclonal antibody against EGFR. Only effective in KRAS wild-type tumors (mutant KRAS signals downstream of EGFR regardless of blockade). Acneiform rash is common.
new: Monoclonal antibody against EGFR. Only effective in RAS (KRAS and NRAS) wild-type, BRAF V600E wild-type, typically left-sided tumors (mutant KRAS signals downstream of EGFR regardless of blockade). Acneiform rash is common.
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: Colon: colonoscopy q10yr starting at 45. Lung: annual LDCT for 50-80yo with ≥20 pack-year history. Breast: mammography starting at 40 (USPSTF 2024). Cervix: Pap q3yr 21-29, cotesting q5yr 30-65.
new: Colon: colonoscopy q10yr starting at 45. Lung: annual LDCT for 50-80yo with ≥20 pack-year history. Breast: mammography starting at 40 (USPSTF 2024). Cervix: cytology q3yr age 21-29; age 30-65 primary HPV testing q5yr (ACS 2020; USPSTF 2024 draft preferred), cotesting q5yr, or cytology q3yr.
rationale: Primary HPV testing is now preferred by ACS (2020) and the 2024 USPSTF draft.
subject: Hematology/Oncology

old: Colorectal: 45 for all. Breast: mammography 40-50 (shared decision), biennial 50-74. Cervical: Pap at 21, co-testing 30-65. Lung: LDCT 50-80 with 20+ pack-year history.
new: Colorectal: 45 for all. Breast: USPSTF 2024 biennial mammography ages 40-74 (ACS: annual 45-54, option to start at 40). Cervical: cytology from 21; HPV-based testing for 30-65. Lung: LDCT 50-80 with 20+ pack-year history.
rationale: Card labeled 2024-2025 but states the superseded 2016 USPSTF breast recommendation; contradicts ob148 and he181.
subject: Multisystem / Mixed

old: Pap screening: 21-29 (Pap alone q3yr), 30-65 (Pap + HPV co-testing q5yr). ASCUS + HPV → colposcopy. CIN 2/3 → LEEP or cold knife cone.
new: Screening: cytology q3yr age 21-29; age 30-65 primary HPV q5yr (ACS 2020; USPSTF 2024 draft), cotesting q5yr, or cytology q3yr. ASCUS + HPV → colposcopy. CIN 2/3 → LEEP or cold knife cone.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Type III hypersensitivity. ANA sensitive (>95%), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith specific. 11 ACR criteria, need 4+.
new: Type III hypersensitivity. ANA sensitive (>95%), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith specific. 2019 EULAR/ACR classification: ANA ≥1:80 entry criterion plus weighted domains totaling ≥10 points (older: 11 ACR criteria with ≥4; SLICC 2012).
subject: Rheumatology

old: Never start allopurinol during acute flare
new: ACR 2020: urate-lowering therapy can be started during a flare (with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis); do not stop it if already taking
rationale: Contradicts ACR 2020; appears in five cards (rh001, rh033, rh034, rh096, rh102).
subject: Rheumatology

old: Colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerization → decreased neutrophil migration. First-line if NSAIDs contraindicated. GI side effects (diarrhea).
new: Colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerization → decreased neutrophil migration. Colchicine, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids are all first-line for a flare (ACR 2020). GI side effects (diarrhea).
rationale: ACR 2020 does not rank colchicine behind NSAIDs.
subject: Rheumatology

old: Never start allopurinol during acute attack
new: ACR 2020: ULT may be started during a flare with prophylaxis
subject: Rheumatology

old: First-line chronic gout. Lower uric acid target <6 mg/dL. Do NOT start during acute attack. Rash → SJS risk (check HLA-B*5801).
new: First-line chronic gout. Lower uric acid target <6 mg/dL. Can be started during an acute flare with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis (ACR 2020); start low (≤100 mg/day) and titrate. Rash → SJS risk (check HLA-B*5801).
subject: Rheumatology

old: Do NOT start during acute attack — can worsen flare
new: ACR 2020: starting ULT during a flare does not need to be delayed (use prophylaxis)
subject: Rheumatology

old: NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen) or colchicine for acute gout. Steroids if both contraindicated. Never start urate-lowering therapy during acute attack.
new: NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen) or colchicine for acute gout. Steroids if both contraindicated. ACR 2020: all three (NSAID, colchicine, glucocorticoid) are first-line, and ULT can be started during a flare with prophylaxis.
subject: Rheumatology

old: Never start allopurinol during acute flare
new: ACR 2020: ULT can be started during a flare; if already on allopurinol, do not stop
subject: Rheumatology

old: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor → decreases uric acid production. Start after acute flare resolves. Target uric acid <6 mg/dL.
new: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor → decreases uric acid production. Can be started during a flare with prophylaxis (ACR 2020). Target uric acid <6 mg/dL.
subject: Rheumatology

old: Stop methotrexate 3 months before conception
new: ACR 2020 reproductive guideline: stop methotrexate at least 1 month before conception (older EULAR advice: 3 months)
rationale: Interval differs between ACR 2020 and older sources.
subject: Rheumatology

old: Nintedanib approved for RA-associated ILD
new: Nintedanib is FDA-approved for chronic fibrosing ILDs with a progressive phenotype (including RA-ILD) and for SSc-ILD
subject: Rheumatology

old: First-line treatment: exercise + weight loss + acetaminophen
new: ACR 2019: exercise and weight loss first; topical (knee) and oral NSAIDs preferred drugs; acetaminophen only conditionally recommended
subject: Rheumatology

old: Recombinant PTH analog (PTH 1-34). Anabolic — stimulates osteoblasts. Limited to 2 years due to osteosarcoma risk in animal studies.
new: Recombinant PTH analog (PTH 1-34). Anabolic — stimulates osteoblasts. Typically limited to about 2 years; the FDA removed the osteosarcoma boxed warning in 2020.
subject: Rheumatology

old: No cervical change for ≥6 hours with adequate contractions (Montevideo units ≥200). Cesarean delivery if truly arrested.
new: Active-phase arrest (≥6 cm with ruptured membranes): no cervical change for ≥4 hours with adequate contractions (>200 MVU) or ≥6 hours with inadequate contractions despite oxytocin (ACOG/SMFM 2014). Cesarean delivery if truly arrested.
rationale: The 2014 consensus shortened the arrest definition to 4 hours.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: ≥6 hours with adequate contractions and no change = arrest
new: ≥4 hours of adequate contractions (or ≥6 hours of inadequate contractions with oxytocin) at ≥6 cm = arrest
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: β-hCG above discriminatory zone (~2000) without IUP. Ampulla most common site. Methotrexate if stable and unruptured.
new: β-hCG above the discriminatory zone (traditionally 1,500-2,000; ACOG 2018 notes up to 3,500 mIU/mL) without IUP. Ampulla most common site. Methotrexate if stable and unruptured.
rationale: Higher threshold avoids interrupting viable IUPs.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: β-hCG >2000 without IUP on TVUS = ectopic until proven otherwise
new: β-hCG above the discriminatory level (about 1,500-3,500) without IUP on TVUS = ectopic until proven otherwise; no threshold should delay TVUS
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: Planned cesarean at 35-37 weeks if diagnosed prenatally
new: Planned cesarean at 34 0/7-37 0/7 weeks if diagnosed prenatally (ACOG)
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Pruritus (especially palms/soles) with elevated serum bile acids. Risk of fetal demise. Ursodeoxycholic acid treatment. Deliver at 36-37 weeks.
new: Pruritus (especially palms/soles) with elevated serum bile acids. Risk of fetal demise. Ursodeoxycholic acid treatment. Timing of delivery depends on bile acid level (SMFM 2021): ≥100 µmol/L at 36 weeks; 40-99 at 36-39 weeks; <40 at 39 weeks.
rationale: SMFM stratified delivery timing by bile acids.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Deliver at 36-37 weeks due to risk of sudden fetal demise
new: Delivery timing is stratified by bile acids (≥100 µmol/L: 36 weeks; 40-99: 36-39 weeks; <40: 39 weeks)
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Local progestin effect. Mirena 7 years, Liletta 8 years. Also treats menorrhagia, endometrial hyperplasia. Can cause amenorrhea (beneficial side effect).
new: Local progestin effect. Mirena 8 years (FDA 2022), Liletta 8 years. Also treats menorrhagia, endometrial hyperplasia. Can cause amenorrhea (beneficial side effect).
rationale: Mirena extended from 7 to 8 years in 2022.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: IUDs: copper (non-hormonal, 10yr) and levonorgestrel (hormonal, 3-7yr depending on type). Implant (etonogestrel, 3yr). >99% effective.
new: IUDs: copper (non-hormonal, 10yr) and levonorgestrel (hormonal, 3-8yr depending on type). Implant (etonogestrel, 3yr). >99% effective.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Planned cesarean hysterectomy at 34-36 weeks
new: Planned cesarean hysterectomy at 34 0/7-35 6/7 weeks (ACOG)
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Do NOT attempt manual removal (catastrophic hemorrhage). Planned cesarean hysterectomy at 34-36 weeks with placenta left untouched. Requires blood products, urology, IR available.
new: Do NOT attempt manual removal (catastrophic hemorrhage). Planned cesarean hysterectomy at 34 0/7-35 6/7 weeks with placenta left untouched. Requires blood products, urology, IR available.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Planned delivery at 34-36 weeks
new: Planned delivery at 34 0/7-35 6/7 weeks
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Ectopic endometrial tissue. Laparoscopy is gold standard diagnosis. Medical: OCPs, GnRH agonists, progestins. Surgical: excision/ablation.
new: Ectopic endometrial tissue. Diagnosis can be clinical plus imaging (TVUS/MRI); laparoscopy is no longer required before empiric treatment (ESHRE 2022; ACOG 2021). Medical: OCPs, GnRH agonists, progestins. Surgical: excision/ablation.
rationale: Guidelines moved away from mandatory surgical diagnosis.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Laparoscopy is gold standard for diagnosis
new: Laparoscopy with histology is the definitive test, but clinical/imaging diagnosis with empiric therapy is now standard
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Ovarian failure before age 40. Elevated FSH (>40) on two occasions 4 weeks apart. Causes: autoimmune, Turner mosaicism, fragile X premutation, iatrogenic (chemo/radiation).
new: Ovarian failure before age 40. FSH >25 IU/L on two occasions >4 weeks apart (ESHRE; older criterion >40). Causes: autoimmune, Turner mosaicism, fragile X premutation, iatrogenic (chemo/radiation).
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: FSH >40 mIU/mL on two occasions confirms diagnosis
new: FSH >25 IU/L on two occasions >4 weeks apart confirms diagnosis (ESHRE; older teaching >40)
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: ART (combination antiretroviral therapy) throughout pregnancy. Viral load at 36 weeks: <1000 → vaginal delivery OK. ≥1000 → scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks. IV zidovudine intrapartum if viral load detectable.
new: ART (combination antiretroviral therapy) throughout pregnancy. Viral load at 36 weeks: <1000 → vaginal delivery OK. ≥1000 → scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks. IV zidovudine intrapartum if viral load >1,000 copies/mL or unknown (consider at 50-999); not required if ≤50 and adherent.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Most accurate dating: first trimester US (crown-rump length, ±5 days). Second trimester: ±2 weeks. Third trimester: ±3 weeks. If US and LMP differ by >7 days in first trimester, use US dates.
new: Most accurate dating: first trimester US (crown-rump length, ±5 days). Second trimester: ±2 weeks. Third trimester: ±3 weeks. ACOG 2017: redate by CRL when discrepancy is >5 days at <9 0/7 weeks or >7 days at 9 0/7-13 6/7 weeks.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Hysteroscopic resection is minimally invasive and improves outcomes
new: Hysteroscopic resection is minimally invasive, but randomized evidence that it improves live birth is limited and conflicting (ESHRE suggests considering after counseling)
rationale: Benefit of septum resection is debated.
subject: Obstetrics/Gynecology

old: Use hour-specific bilirubin nomogram to decide on phototherapy
new: Use the 2022 AAP phototherapy thresholds (age in hours, gestational age, neurotoxicity risk factors), which replaced the 2004 Bhutani-based curves
subject: Pediatrics

old: EDTA chelation for levels ≥45; dimercaprol + EDTA for levels ≥70
new: Chelation at BLL ≥45 µg/dL (oral succimer); dimercaprol + CaNa2EDTA for ≥70 µg/dL or encephalopathy
rationale: Oral succimer is used for 45-69; the CDC blood lead reference value is now 3.5 µg/dL.
subject: Pediatrics

old: Most common preventable cause of intellectual disability
new: A leading preventable cause of intellectual disability (alongside fetal alcohol spectrum disorder)
subject: Pediatrics

old: HepB is the only vaccine given at birth
new: HepB is the only routine birth vaccine (AAP recommends it for all medically stable newborns; the federal CDC schedule revised in Dec 2025-Jan 2026 moved it to individual decision-making for infants of HBsAg-negative mothers)
rationale: Federal and AAP schedules diverged in 2025-2026; verify which source the target exam follows.
subject: Pediatrics

old: Screen for Wilms tumor with abdominal US every 3 months until age 8
new: Screen for Wilms tumor with abdominal US every 3 months until the 7th birthday (AACR 2017)
rationale: AACR BWS screening ends at age 7 (verify).
subject: Pediatrics

old: Most common at birth in premature boys. If not descended by 6 months → orchiopexy by 12 months. Increased risk of testicular cancer and infertility.
new: Most common at birth in premature boys. If not descended by 6 months → orchiopexy between 6 and 18 months of corrected age (AUA 2014). Increased risk of testicular cancer and infertility.
subject: Pediatrics

old: If not descended by 6 months, unlikely to descend spontaneously. Orchiopexy by 12 months to preserve fertility and reduce (but not eliminate) cancer risk.
new: If not descended by 6 months, unlikely to descend spontaneously. Orchiopexy between 6 and 18 months of corrected age (AUA 2014) to preserve fertility and reduce (but not eliminate) cancer risk.
subject: Surgery

old: SLNB recommended for melanoma >1mm Breslow depth or with ulceration. Positive SLNB = complete lymph node dissection.
new: SLNB recommended for melanoma >1mm Breslow depth or with ulceration. A positive SLNB no longer mandates completion lymph node dissection (MSLT-II); nodal ultrasound surveillance is standard.
rationale: MSLT-II showed no melanoma-specific survival benefit from routine completion dissection.
subject: Surgery

old: Gustilo classification (I-III). Emergent: tetanus, IV antibiotics, irrigation, surgical debridement within 6 hours. Cover wound with sterile saline dressing.
new: Gustilo classification (I-III). Emergent: tetanus, IV antibiotics, irrigation, debridement timed per BOAST-4 (immediate for gross contamination or vascular injury, within 12 hours for high-energy fractures, within 24 hours for others) with antibiotics as early as possible (ideally within 1 hour). Cover wound with sterile saline dressing.
subject: Surgery

old: CTA to identify aneurysm. Nimodipine for vasospasm prevention (days 4-10). Surgical clipping or endovascular coiling.
new: CTA to identify aneurysm. Nimodipine (60 mg q4h for 21 days) improves outcome after SAH; it does not prevent angiographic vasospasm (vasospasm peaks days 4-14). Surgical clipping or endovascular coiling.
rationale: Card contradicts n167 and itself (days 4-10 vs 4-14).
subject: Surgery

old: Nimodipine prevents vasospasm (days 4-14 post-SAH)
new: Nimodipine improves neurologic outcome after SAH (it does not prevent vasospasm); vasospasm peaks days 4-14
subject: Surgery

old: Airway first (intubate if inhalation suspected). Parkland formula: 4mL × kg × %TBSA. Half in first 8 hours from time of burn.
new: Airway first (intubate if inhalation suspected). Parkland formula: 4mL × kg × %TBSA (classic exam answer; current ABLS starts at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA and titrates to urine output). Half in first 8 hours from time of burn.
rationale: Teaching vs current practice; low priority.
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: Narrow therapeutic index. Hypokalemia increases toxicity. Treat with Digibind (Fab fragments). Avoid calcium (worsens toxicity).
new: Narrow therapeutic index. Hypokalemia increases toxicity. Treat with Digibind (Fab fragments). IV calcium is no longer considered contraindicated for hyperkalemia in digoxin toxicity (the "stone heart" concern is not supported by data).
rationale: Retrospective data (Levine 2011) show no excess arrhythmia/mortality; still a popular board point, so verify target exam.
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: AVOID IV calcium in digoxin toxicity (stone heart)
new: "Stone heart" is not supported: retrospective data show no excess arrhythmia or mortality with IV calcium; digoxin Fab is definitive treatment
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: Rochester/Philadelphia/Step-by-Step criteria identify low-risk infants. Low-risk: blood, urine, ± LP based on protocol. May observe without antibiotics if truly low-risk. High-risk: full workup + empiric antibiotics.
new: AAP 2021 (8-60 days) and the PECARN rule risk-stratify well-appearing febrile infants using urinalysis, ANC, CRP and procalcitonin (PCT >0.5 ng/mL, CRP >20 mg/L, ANC >4,000 guide LP and antibiotics); Rochester/Philadelphia/Step-by-Step are older criteria. Low-risk: blood, urine, ± LP based on protocol. May observe without antibiotics if truly low-risk. High-risk: full workup + empiric antibiotics.
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: 29-90 days: risk-stratify. <28 days: ALL get full workup + antibiotics
new: AAP 2021: 8-21 days = full workup incl. LP + antibiotics + admission; 22-28 days = inflammatory markers guide LP/antibiotics; 29-60 days = risk-stratify with markers
subject: Emergency Medicine

old: Cold nodule with suspicious FNA → total thyroidectomy. Papillary most common thyroid cancer. Excellent prognosis.
new: Cold nodule with suspicious FNA → thyroidectomy: lobectomy is acceptable for low-risk papillary cancer ≤4 cm (ATA 2015); total thyroidectomy for >4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, nodal or distant disease. Papillary most common thyroid cancer. Excellent prognosis.
rationale: ATA 2015 de-escalated surgery for low-risk tumors.
subject: Surgery

old: HAD 2 Gs: H2, Alpha(nope—wrong), D1 — Beta-1/2 are the classic Gs
new: Gs-coupled receptors include β1, β2, D1, H2 and V2 (also glucagon, TSH, ACTH and PTH receptors)
rationale: Pearl contains broken text ("Alpha(nope—wrong)") and no usable mnemonic.
subject: Multisystem / Mixed

old: p < 0.05 = <5% probability the result is due to chance alone. Does NOT mean clinically significant. Type I error (alpha) = rejecting true null.
new: p < 0.05: if the null hypothesis were true, a result at least this extreme would occur <5% of the time (it is not the probability that chance explains the result). Does NOT mean clinically significant. Type I error (alpha) = rejecting true null.
subject: Multisystem / Mixed

old: Clean wounds: primary closure within 6-8h (12-24h for face). Irrigate copiously. Assess tetanus status. Tdap if >5 years for dirty wounds.
new: No strict golden period: well-irrigated clean wounds can often be closed primarily well beyond 6-8 h (face up to 24 h), depending on contamination and location. Irrigate copiously. Assess tetanus status. Tdap if >5 years for dirty wounds.
source: General wound-closure evidence (Quinn et al., Ann Emerg Med 2014; no URL)
subject: Emergency Medicine
